s1.eyebrow: A decision game on real Geneva data
s1.title: Where should the bikes live?
s1.lede: Geneva wants shared bikes that work with its trams and buses, not against them. Behind this demo is an optimisation model that decides, on a budget, where to open stations, how many docks each gets and how many bikes start the day there, so that as much potential demand as possible is served — by bike alone or by bike plus public transport. It answers four questions a city asks.
s1.f1: potential trips a day, between the zones of the study area — an upper bound of who could use the bikes, not a forecast
s1.f2: candidate station sites: the zone centres, plus the public-transport stops that could host a transfer station
s1.f3: periods in the model's day — morning, midday, evening — because bikes end up where people went
s1.paper: Research: Z. Wu, S. Sharif Azadeh, L. Brotcorne — Network Design of Bike Sharing Systems with Public Transport Integration, INOCS (Inria Lille) & TU Delft, EU SUM project. The demo uses the model exactly as submitted; demand here is counted from observed shared-bike trips, where the paper estimates it from a public-transport survey and ridership.
s2.title: Watch the city live
s2.lede: Drag through a day or press play. The red circles on the map grow with boardings and alightings. Find the pattern a planner has to serve — and see how the model summarises it.
s2.f1: public-transport boardings on a typical Monday ({sun} on a Sunday)
s2.f2: Monday's commute peaks. Sundays have no morning peak at all
s2.f3: median observed shared-bike trip — short hops, often to or from transit
s2.f4: shared-bike trips a day observed on this day type today — small, and that is the point
s2.ins.mon.0: The city sleeps — almost nothing moves before 6h.
s2.ins.mon.1: Morning rush: flows pour into Cornavin and Bel-Air. Bikes parked here tonight will be gone by 9h.
s2.ins.mon.2: Midday hum — steadier, spread across the centre and the university.
s2.ins.mon.3: The day's biggest peak, 17–18h: everyone heads home at once. Docks fill up fast downtown.
s2.ins.mon.4: Evening wind-down along the lake and Plainpalais.
s2.ins.sun.0: No morning peak on Sundays — the commute pattern simply isn't there.
s2.ins.sun.1: A slow start: leisure trips build through the late morning.
s2.ins.sun.2: Sunday peaks at 16–18h — lakeside and old-town leisure, not commuting.
s2.ins.sun.3: A quiet evening. A network tuned only for Monday would waste money today.
s2.model.h: How the model sees this day: three periods, each with its share of the trips — the paper's “temporal demand profile”. These weights are the ones observed in the Geneva trip data for the selected day type.
s2.model.baseline: The paper's baseline uses a bimodal profile instead ({w}), so a plan solved for it targets two commuting peaks rather than Geneva's observed evening-heavy day.
s2.note: Ridership: public-transport operator data, per stop × hour × weekday. Bike trips: operator data, Jun–Dec 2024. The hourly animation illustrates the rhythm; the model itself solves the three periods above.
s2.cta: You've seen where Geneva moves. Take the budget →

s4.howbox.btn: How the model decides — in the paper's terms
s4.howbox.l1: Each potential trip ({demand} a day, per origin–destination pair and period) can take one of up to three pre-computed routes: bike only, or bike + tram/bus (bike to a stop, ride, bike again). Routes within 20 % of the fastest option are kept; shorter routes are preferred.
s4.howbox.l2: A route counts only if it works: every station on it is built, a bike is in stock at the start station in that period, and a dock is free at the end. Otherwise the trip is not served — the rider stays on foot or on public transport. Nothing is drawn at random: the model chooses the assignment that serves the most trips within the budget.
s4.howbox.l3: Bikes end up where people went. Between periods the model moves bikes from full to empty stations; a truck carries 10 bikes, so runs per day = bikes moved ÷ 10, rounded up per station pair; each run costs 40 € + 10 € per km, capped by the daily operating budget. A small penalty (ε = {eps}) discards runs that add no served trip. This plan: {runs} run(s) moving {bikes} bikes.
s4.chart.sub: Potential trips (grey) against trips served, split by how they travel.
s4.chart.alt: Potential and served trips per model period
s4.reading.starter: With {budget} the network is a seed, not a system: {morning} of the morning and {evening} of the evening period are served, and only {pt} of the served trips touch public transport — the model buys bike-only coverage first and reaches the tram and bus stops only with more money. {delta} fewer trips are served than with the {refname}.
s4.reading.essential: With {budget} the model has to triage: it serves {morning} of the morning but only {evening} of the evening period, and only {pt} of the served trips touch public transport. Whole neighbourhoods stay without a station.
s4.reading.reference: The evening period carries the largest share of the day, and {evening} of it is served. {pt} of served trips connect to a tram or a bus — the network has crossed into genuine public-transport integration.
s4.reading.ambitious: Almost the same day as the {refname}: the extra money lifts served demand by {delta} trips. Docks nearly double, but those riders were already served.
s5.title: Compare plans
s5.lede: The four questions of step 1, answered from the runs. Open a card to see the proof: one chart per question, solid marks for the runs made, hollow marks for the runs still to come.
s5.q.nodata: Not enough runs on disk yet to answer this from the data — the proof below shows which ones are missing.
s5.q1.why: That is where the curve bends: {lo} already serves {plo} of the demand, {hi} serves {phi}. The next {more} add only {pts} points, while each served trip costs {c2} of investment instead of {c1}.
s5.q2.why: The biggest jump in the budget ladder: trips combining bike and PT go from {s1} to {s2} of served trips as transfer stations grow from {t1} to {t2}. After that the share levels off ({s3} at {top}).
s5.q3.ans: Docks, plus a few truck runs
s5.q3.why: The docks alone serve {p0}. {runs} truck runs a day ({cost}) lift it to {p1}. Spending {topcost} a day on trucks adds only {extra2} more trips.
s5.q4.ans: The service more than the map
s5.q4.why: Every rhythm builds {smin} to {smax} stations. What changes is how much is served: {pb} on a “{best}” day, {pw} on a “{worst}” day, whose {period} peak is only {ps} served.
s5.q3.concl: With {budget} of capital and {base}, the network serves {p0}. {runs} truck runs a day ({cost}) lift it to {p1}: {extra} more trips. Spending {topcost} ({topruns} runs) adds only {extra2} more. Docks stay between {dmin} and {dmax} in every version: trucks add service on top of the docks, they do not replace them.
s5.q3.read: The same {budget} network, from no trucks at all to trucks spending the whole daily operating budget. Both charts share the x axis: the version's capital budget and what limits its trucks.
s5.q3.cost: What the trucks cost, € a day
s5.q3.extra: Trips a day gained over “{base}” (label: gain · share of all trips served)
s5.q3.same: {n} versions with a bigger daily truck budget ({min} to {max}) produce exactly the same solution: {runs} runs, {cost}. The budget is never the limit — the penalty ε on each run is what decides how many are worth making.
s5.q3.note: The paper's finding (Fig. 7–8): an unpenalised model dispatches far more trucks for almost no extra served demand; a small penalty keeps the few runs that matter. These runs locate that trade-off on Geneva data.
s5.q4.concl: A {best} day serves {pb}, a {worst} day only {pw}, with the same {budget}. The busier the peak, the less of it is served: in the {worst} rhythm the {period} carries {share} of the day's trips and {ps} of them are served.
s5.q4.read: The same budget optimised for four rhythms of the day. In each panel the model's three periods are on the x axis: the bar is the period's share of the day's trips, the filled part is how much of it the network serves.
s5.q4.share: Share of the day's potential trips
s5.q4.served: of which served (the % under each period)
s5.q4.alt: Share of daily trips and share served per period, one panel per rhythm
s5.q4.nn.note: The map itself barely moves: whichever the rhythm, a built station stands {nmin}–{nmax} m from its nearest neighbour and the plan builds {smin} to {smax} stations. What the rhythm changes is which periods get served.
s5.q4.note: Weekends: the model has no Sunday run yet — the rhythms above are the paper's three profiles plus Geneva's observed weekday.
s5.q1.concl: From {b1} to {b2}, served demand jumps from {p1} to {p2}. The next {b3} adds {pts} points. Each daily served trip costs {c1}, then {c2}, then {c3} of investment.
s5.q2.concl: At {b1} the system is essentially bike-only: {s1} of served trips touch public transport. At {b2}, {s2} do. The flip happens somewhere between.
s5.q1.alt: Share of potential demand served, against the investment budget
s5.q1.axis: Trips served, % of potential demand, against investment
s5.q1.note: The first euros buy coverage: a small network already serves a third of the demand. Past the reference plan, extra money buys docks for riders who were already served — the paper's diminishing returns.
s5.q2.alt: Share of served trips that are PT-assisted, against the investment budget
s5.q2.axis: Share of served trips that combine bike and public transport, against investment
s5.q2.note: Below the threshold the model concentrates its few stations on the densest direct-cycling pairs; above it, it can afford transfer stations at tram and bus stops, and PT-assisted trips take off. The paper calls this a regime transition and advises locating it before investing, “to strengthen the PT network rather than merely complement it”.
s5.all.note: Advanced columns: OD pairs covered (share of the origin–destination pairs with any served flow) and the mean nearest-neighbour distance between built stations. Italic rows are scenarios whose run has still to be made.

story.lambda: Path penalty λ · routes per OD pair
story.lambda.v: 0.1 · up to 3, within 20 % of the fastest
story.src: Unit costs, path penalty and capacity bounds are the model's own constants, quoted from the paper's Table D.8; every other row is read from the scenario configuration and from the run's own record.
how.served.p: The model receives a potential demand of {demand} trips a day between the zones of the study area, split into three periods. It decides which stations to open, their docks and their morning stock, and assigns each trip to one of up to three pre-computed routes (bike only, or bike + tram/bus) — a route is usable only if every station on it is built and has a bike to take and a dock to leave it in. “Trips served” is the total assigned flow divided by the potential demand, exactly the objective the paper maximises. Potential demand is an upper bound (the paper: “a proxy for potential multimodal demand, not a prediction that all passengers would switch”).
how.pt.h: How “connected to public transport” is computed
how.pt.p: Among served trips, those assigned to a bike + public-transport route (bike to a stop, ride, and optionally bike again) divided by all served trips. The paper reports this as the share of served demand routed through PT-assisted paths, and shows that it jumps once the budget crosses a threshold.
how.time.h: How “time saved per trip” is computed
how.time.p: For each served trip the model knows the travel time of its route and the time of the best alternative without bikes (walking, or walking + public transport). The difference, averaged over served trips and weighted by flow, is the time saved ({gain} min here); the percentage ({saving}) relates it to that alternative. The paper reports about 4.4 minutes and 48 % for its baseline, and suggests cities multiply this by their value of time for a cost–benefit appraisal.
how.ops.p: The model plans, per period, how many bikes to move between which stations and how many truck runs that takes (a truck carries 10 bikes; a run costs 40 € plus 10 € per km). The daily operating budget caps this spending, and a small penalty ε in the objective discourages runs that do not add served trips.

scen.budget_020k.name: Starter budget
scen.budget_020k.pitch: The city tests the water with the smallest budget on this page — what does a seed network buy, and what does it leave out?
scen.budget_020k.narrative: Twenty thousand euros is below the range the study examines (Table 2); this run was added to locate the point where public-transport integration begins (Fig. 14). With so little money the optimiser buys coverage first: a few small stations at the zone centres that carry the most demand, and only a handful at public-transport stops. Read this plan as the seed every other plan grows from — a bike-only service for a fraction of the potential riders, against which each extra euro of the larger budgets can be measured.
scen.budget_060k.name: Essential plan
scen.budget_060k.pitch: The city invests the minimum of the paper's range — who is left out?
scen.budget_060k.narrative: Sixty thousand euros is the smallest budget the study examines. The optimiser has to triage: it buys the stations and docks that carry the most demand and puts them where cycling and public transport reinforce each other, leaving the thinner corridors uncovered. Read this plan for what a minimal investment cannot reach — which neighbourhoods stay outside the network, and how much of the potential demand goes unserved.
scen.budget_080k.name: Reference plan
scen.budget_080k.pitch: The paper's baseline: 80 000 € of investment, 5 % of it kept for daily operations.
scen.budget_080k.narrative: This is the configuration the published study uses as its reference (Table D.8): 80 000 € of capital, an operational envelope of 5 % for moving bikes around, three demand periods and a moderate penalty on truck dispatches. Every other plan on this page changes exactly one of those settings, so whatever differs is attributable to that one change.
scen.budget_120k.name: Ambitious plan
scen.budget_120k.pitch: Is more always better? Twice the essential budget, and the returns start to flatten.
scen.budget_120k.narrative: At 120 000 € the city buys the top of the paper's range. Nearly every zone gets a station and the network reaches deep into the tram and bus map — but each additional euro buys fewer newly served trips than the one before it. Put the served share and the investment per served trip next to the reference plan: the gap between them is the diminishing return the model exists to quantify.
scen.S1_essential.name: Essential network
scen.S1_essential.pitch: The city invests the bare minimum. Where do the few stations go — and who is left out?
scen.S1_essential.narrative: With a small budget the optimisation model has to triage: it concentrates stations where demand and public-transport connections pay off most, leaving whole neighbourhoods uncovered. This is a legacy run: it uses Geneva's observed period weights and a 2.5 % operating budget, where the paper's grid uses the bimodal profile and 5 %.
scen.S2_balanced.name: Balanced network
scen.S2_balanced.pitch: A solid network at the budget the research studied for Geneva. Most potential riders get a bike, and four in ten served trips connect to a tram or a bus.
scen.S2_balanced.narrative: The configuration of the published Geneva proof-of-concept — 80 000 € of investment, 2.5 % of it for operations — with one change: the demand period weights are the ones observed in the real trip data instead of the paper's bimodal profile, so the design targets Geneva's actual morning and evening peaks. It is superseded by the paper's own baseline once that run exists.
scen.S3_ambitious.name: Ambitious network
scen.S3_ambitious.pitch: Nearly every zone gets a station and the operating budget doubles. Is more always better?
scen.S3_ambitious.narrative: Nearly every zone gets a station, and the operating envelope doubles, so almost no rider is turned away. The metrics show diminishing returns: each extra euro buys fewer additional served trips, and the investment per served trip rises. Quantifying that trade-off is exactly what the optimisation model is for.
